title: How To Handle A Student Who Begs For A Second Chance
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the moment a student pleads for an exception — a fixed grade, a forgiven infraction, a redo — and argues that giving in, however tempting and well-intentioned it feels, is a serious mistake. He identifies three costs: caving to one student forces an unequal, resentment-breeding double standard once other students notice; each concession makes the next 'no' harder to hold, gradually turning a teacher into a pushover besieged by special requests; and a reputation for lowered standards drains the teacher's words of authority, forcing them into escalating tactics like raised voices and countdowns. His prescribed solution is to say no immediately, framing each refusal as a lesson that builds student strength over time, and arguing that fixed, unwavering standards make teaching easier overall by removing a whole category of stress and negotiation.
points: Giving in to a student's plea for an exception, however well-intentioned, sets a costly precedent.
Caving to one student creates an unequal standard that breeds resentment once other students notice.
Each concession makes the next 'no' harder, gradually turning a teacher into a besieged pushover.
A reputation for lowered standards drains a teacher's words of authority, forcing escalating tactics like raised voices.
The recommended response is to say no immediately, framing each refusal as a lesson that builds student resilience.
quotes: A student comes to you and begs for a second chance. They swear that from now on things will be different.
If you cave to even one student, you better allow the same lower standard for everyone else or it will come back to bite you.
Knuckle under just once and chinks in your armor will begin to show, the steel growing soft and malleable. Saying no gets harder and harder.
With a reputation for lowering the bar, your words will lack punch. They’ll be devoid of urgency, meaning, and the power to get students moving, working, and listening.
It also engenders trust, respect, and likability. It supports social, emotional, and academic growth and maturity.
